source: Over the past few generations, work in America has become far less physical. A lot of farming and factory work was replaced by desk jobs. In turn, work became less backbreaking—and less dangerous.
why: The file is a current cross-section of occupations; it has no historical time series on the physical demands or composition of work.
data.csv contains one current injury rate per occupation, not the 1970–2022 national fatality and injury series shown in the chart.

source: For most of American history, people worked until their bodies gave out. In 1900, most men older than 65 still worked to be self-sufficient, including 84% of Black Americans.
why: The file has no historical labor-force participation data by age or race.

why: The file has no historical labor-force participation series for older men by race.

source: Since the mid-1990s, undocumented immigrants haven't received Social Security benefits, even though they pay taxes to fund the system. Many will never be able to retire.
why: data.csv has a noncitizen workforce share but no immigration-status, benefit-eligibility or retirement data.

source: The history of labor in America is defined by the least privileged people doing the least desirable work—sometimes by force.
why: Qualitative historical claim; the file contains no historical evidence on privilege, coercion or labor history.
